intro: People seated round a triangular table: three at the corners and three in the middle of the sides, or a corner and two persons on each side. These lessons follow the same method as the other seating topics, with one difference that matters: **no real exam puzzle of this kind was found**, so everything here is built from your bank.

**What I studied.** 28 memory-based papers that have a Reasoning section (16 IBPS Clerk Prelims from 2016 to October 2025, 12 SBI Clerk, RRB Clerk and IBPS PO Prelims), plus 14 shift-analysis pages listing the puzzles of IBPS Clerk 2023 to 2025, SBI Clerk 2025 and RRB Clerk 2024 to 2025 shifts. Then every triangular set in your bank: 24 Guidely puzzles and 7 Sreedhar ones (28 different puzzles; three are printed twice). Each was written out as exact conditions and solved by a script that tried every seating.
| Triangular sets in the real papers and shift lists | 0 (the seating sets there were circles, squares, rows and parallel rows) |
| Bank puzzles with exactly one arrangement | 31 of 31 (3 only after a stated reading of a missing opening line) |
| Bank questions whose key matched the script | 153 of 153 (for 3 questions only under a stated reading) |
| Table shapes (28 different puzzles) | 6 seats, corners and middles: 16 (2 with an empty seat); 9 seats, corners and two a side: 9 (2 with an empty seat); people on the sides only: 3 |
| Facing | all to the centre 14; corners out and middles in 8; corners in and middles out 3; all outside 2; decided by clues 1 |
| Puzzles where a clue names one person's seat type (corner, middle or facing) | 24 of 28 |
| A second fact per person (places, animals, ages, brands) | 6 of 28 |
| Cases left by the best two-person opening clue | 1 case in 7 puzzles, 2 in 13, 3 or more in 3 (23 puzzles measured) |
| First printed clue already the best opening | 11 of 18 single-fact puzzles; the printed order cost 46 cases in all against 34 for the best order |

**What this means.** A triangle with three corners and three middles is a circle of six where the seats alternate: corner, middle, corner, middle. That one fact gives you a free clue in almost every set, because a step of one or three seats changes the seat type and a step of two keeps it. And in 24 of the 28 puzzles someone is named as sitting at a corner or in a middle, so you can seat that person first without any cases.

A note on honesty: I did not find this puzzle in any IBPS Clerk, SBI Clerk, RRB Clerk or IBPS PO paper or shift list I could open, so every archetype here is **Bank only**. Several shift-analysis sites blocked my reader, so a triangular set in a shift I did not open cannot be ruled out. Memory-based papers are reconstructions. Give this topic less time than circles, squares and rows.
after: That is the triangular table as your bank sets it. The **Quick revision** tab has the same material as short notes, drills and a practice ladder.

The order of work for every set: number the seats from the top corner, mark IN or OUT, seat the person with a seat-type clue first, take the clue that joins that person to one more, use odd and even steps to kill cases, and keep "not a neighbour" clues for the last seats.
No triangular, pentagonal or hexagonal set was found in the clerk papers opened. If time is short, study circles, squares and rows first.

lessons.title: Six seats: corners and middles take turns
lessons.plain: The starting point. Number the six seats round the triangle; corners are the odd seats, middles the even ones, and every clue becomes a step of so many seats.
teach: Three persons sit at the corners and three in the middle of the sides. Go round the table and the seats take turns: corner, middle, corner, middle, corner, middle. So it is a circle of six with a label on every seat.
**How to draw it.** Draw a triangle with one corner at the top. Number the seats **1 to 6 clockwise from the top corner**. Seats 1, 3 and 5 are corners; seats 2, 4 and 6 are middles.

**Left and right.** When everyone faces the centre, a person's **left is the next seat clockwise (+1)** and their right is the next seat anticlockwise (-1). Left and right belong to the person named after "of".
| The clue says | Seats apart | Seat type |
| Immediate left or right | 1 | changes |
| Second to the left or right, or one person between | 2 | stays the same |
| Third to the left or right, two persons between, or opposite | 3 | changes |
**Opposite** on this table means three seats on: a corner faces the middle of the far side. Second to the left and fourth to the right are the same seat, which is why options say "Both 1 and 3".

**Where to start.** All three corners look the same, and so do all three middles. So when a clue says "X sits at a corner", put X at seat 1; for "X sits in the middle of a side", put X at seat 2. No cases are lost by doing this. In 24 of the 28 bank puzzles such a clue is given.

Then take a clue that names that person and one other. "Second to the left of" fixes the other person in one seat; "one person sits between" gives two seats, so draw the table twice and kill one drawing with a neighbour or a seat-type clue.

example.q: No triangular puzzle was found in the real papers, so this is a bank set (Sreedhar model test 54). Six persons San, Sel, Ski, Sum, Sya and Sze sit round a triangular table facing the centre, three at the corners and three in the middles of the sides. One person sits between San and Sya. Ski sits second to the right of Sze. Ski does not sit opposite Sya. Sum sits opposite neither Sze nor San, but sits on the immediate left of Sel, who sits at a corner.
steps: Sel sits at a corner: Sel at seat 1. Sum is Sel's immediate left: seat 2.
Sum is opposite seat 5, so seat 5 is neither Sze nor San.
The free seats are 3, 4, 5, 6. The pairs two apart are 3-5 (corners) and 4-6 (middles). San-Sya and Ski-Sze are both pairs two apart, so one takes the corners and the other the middles.
Ski and Sze on the corners: seat 5 must be Ski, Sze 3, and then second to Sze's right is seat 1, Sel. Out.
San and Sya on the corners: seat 5 is Sya, San 3. Ski is second to Sze's right: Sze 6, Ski 4. Ski (4) is opposite Sel, not Sya. Fine.
example.answer: Seats 1 to 6 clockwise from the top corner: Sel, Sum, San, Ski, Sya, Sze.

check.q: Six persons sit round a triangular table facing the centre, three at the corners and three in the middles. X sits at a corner. Y sits third to the left of X. Where does Y sit?

options.b: In the middle of a side

check.why: Three seats is an odd step, and an odd step changes the seat type: Y is in the middle of the far side, opposite X. The tempting wrong answer is "at a corner", from thinking that three steps jump corner to corner, which is true only on the nine-seat table.

shortcut.title: Odd steps flip, even steps keep
text: On the six-seat triangle, a step of 1 or 3 seats moves between a corner and a middle; a step of 2 keeps the type.
So "X is second to the left of Y" tells you X and Y are both corners or both middles before you draw anything, and "X sits opposite Y" tells you exactly one of them is at a corner.
Use it to kill a case at once, and to strike out options in "who sits at a corner" questions.

lessons.title: Corners face out, middles face in
lessons.plain: New: the two seat types face opposite ways. Mark each seat IN or OUT once, and take every left and right from the seat of the person after "of".
teach: In 11 of the 28 bank puzzles the corners and the middles face opposite ways: usually corners outside and middles to the centre, sometimes the reverse. This is the one twist that makes the triangle different from a plain circle.
**The rule.** A person facing the centre has left = +1 (clockwise). A person facing outside has **left = -1 (anticlockwise)** and right = +1.
| Seat | Faces | Left | Right |
| Corner (1, 3, 5), if corners face out | outside | -1 | +1 |
| Middle (2, 4, 6), if middles face in | the centre | +1 | -1 |
Before reading any clue, write OUT beside seats 1, 3, 5 and IN beside 2, 4, 6 (or the reverse, as the puzzle says).
**Facing tells you the seat.** "Gita is facing away from the centre" is a seat-type clue in disguise: Gita sits at a corner. "F does not face outside" puts F in a middle.

**Two persons two seats apart share a type, so they share a facing.** "P is second to the left of K" therefore uses the same direction for P and K. But "immediate left" crosses from one type to the other, so check whose left it is.
When no one is given a seat type, try the most-mentioned person at a corner and then in a middle: two cases, and one usually dies within three clues.

example.q: Bank set (Sreedhar model test 57). Six persons Ram, Gita, Raju, Sita, Siri and Gopi sit round a triangular table: the three at the corners face away from the centre, the three in the middles face the centre. Sita, Gita and Siri are the only women; no three persons of the same gender sit together. Only one person sits between Ram and Siri. Gopi sits second to the left of Siri. Only one person sits between Sita and Raju. Gita faces away from the centre. Gita is an immediate neighbour of Gopi. Sita sits second to the left of Gita.
steps: Corners 1, 3, 5 face OUT (left -1); middles 2, 4, 6 face IN (left +1).
Gita faces away, so she is at a corner: Gita at 1. Sita is second to Gita's left: 1 - 2 = seat 5.
Gopi is next to Gita: seat 2 or 6, a middle. Siri is two seats from Gopi, so Siri is a middle too, facing in: Gopi = Siri + 2. Gopi 2 gives Siri 6; Gopi 6 gives Siri 4.
Ram is two seats from Siri, and Raju two from Sita. Gopi 2, Siri 6: Ram 4, Raju 3; but then Sita, Siri and Gita (5, 6, 1) are three women together. Out.
Gopi 6, Siri 4: Ram 2, Raju 3. Seats 1 to 6 read woman, man, man, woman, woman, man. Fine.
example.answer: Seats 1 to 6: Gita, Ram, Raju, Siri, Sita, Gopi. Gita, Raju and Sita face outside; Ram, Siri and Gopi face the centre.

check.q: Seats 1 to 6 run clockwise from the top corner. Corners (1, 3, 5) face outside; middles face the centre. P sits at seat 3. Which seat is second to the left of P?
check.why: P is at a corner, facing outside, so P's left is anticlockwise: 3 - 2 = seat 1. Seat 5 is the answer you get by treating P as facing the centre.

lessons.title: A second fact per person
lessons.plain: New: each person also likes a place, an animal or has an age. Seat the persons first where clues allow, then treat "the one who likes X" as a person whose name you do not know yet.
teach: Six of the 28 bank puzzles add a second fact to each person: places, animals, ages, brands. All six are on the six-seat table. Most clues then name a fact, not a person: "the one who likes Shimla".
**The method.**
- Start from the person with a seat-type clue, as before.
- Treat "the one who likes Shimla" as a person with a label instead of a name. Steps between labels are steps between seats, exactly as before.
- Write the label inside the seat in small letters, and the name beside it when you learn it.

- A clue that links two descriptions ("S sits second to the left of the one who likes Goa") always means **two different persons**. So S does not like Goa. The same goes for "between R and the one who likes Munnar": R does not like Munnar. One Sreedhar set has three arrangements unless you read it this way.

**Facts with a pattern.** "No two people who like water animals sit together" with three water and three land animals forces them to alternate: all the water animals on the middles or all on the corners. That is a seat-type clue in disguise.
**Ages.** Sum and difference clues (J + N = 66, K and O differ by 8) give a short list of pairs; write the list down and let the seating clues choose.

example.q: Bank set (Guidely triangular two-variable, set 1, questions 6 to 10). Six persons A to F sit round a triangular table facing the centre, three at the corners and three in the middles. Each likes a different cartoon: Flintstones, Pokemon, Popeye, Scooby-Doo, Shinchan, Superman. D sits at a corner, next to the one who likes Flintstones. A sits second to the right of the Flintstones fan and third to the left of the Popeye fan. One person sits between the Popeye fan and E, who sits on the immediate right of the Pokemon fan. The Shinchan fan sits on the immediate left of the Pokemon fan. At least one person sits between the Shinchan fan and B, who likes neither Popeye nor Superman. C sits on the immediate right of F but does not like Flintstones.
steps: D at seat 1 (a corner). Flintstones is next to D: seat 2 or 6.
A is second to the right of Flintstones (-2): Flintstones 2 gives A 6; Flintstones 6 gives A 4. Popeye is opposite A: 3, or 1 (D).
Flintstones 2, A 6, Popeye 3: E is two from Popeye at 5; Pokemon is E + 1 = 6 (A) and Shinchan 1 (D). C = F - 1 leaves C on Flintstones or B next to Shinchan. Out.
Flintstones 6, A 4, D likes Popeye: E is at 3 or 5, and Pokemon = E + 1 must not be Flintstones, so E 3, A likes Pokemon, Shinchan at 5.
B is not next to Shinchan (5): B 2. C = F - 1 with seats 5 and 6 left: F 6 (Flintstones), C 5 (Shinchan). B likes neither Popeye nor Superman: B Scooby-Doo, E Superman.
example.answer: Seats 1 to 6: D Popeye, B Scooby-Doo, E Superman, A Pokemon, C Shinchan, F Flintstones.

lessons.title: Nine seats: a corner and two on each side
lessons.plain: New: nine persons, one at each corner and two along each side. Corners are seats 1, 4 and 7, and a step of three goes from corner to corner.
teach: Nine of the 28 bank puzzles seat nine persons (or eight and an empty seat): one at each corner and two along each side.
**How to draw it.** Number the seats **1 to 9 clockwise from the top corner**. Corners are 1, 4 and 7. The sides are 2-3, 5-6 and 8-9.
| Step | From a corner you reach |
| 1 or 2 | a side seat |
| 3 | the next corner |
| 4 or 5 | a side seat on the far side |
| 6 | the corner after next |
**Seat type works in threes now.** A step of 3 or 6 keeps the seat type. "Two persons sit between A and D" with A at a corner puts D at a corner too.
**Same side.** "X and Y sit on the same side" means one of the pairs 2-3, 5-6, 8-9. A corner seat belongs to no side: seat 3 and seat 4 are neighbours, but only seat 3 is on a side.
Left and right work as before: facing the centre, left is +1. On this table nobody sits exactly opposite anyone, so "opposite" clues do not appear here.

example.q: Bank set (Guidely triangular single variable, set 2, questions 16 to 20; the opening line is missing in the bank but the rest is complete). Nine persons M to U sit round a triangular table, one at each corner and two on each side, all facing the centre. T sits second to the right of M. Three persons sit between M and Q. Q sits at a corner. R sits on the immediate right of P. Neither Q nor M sits next to R. U sits third to the right of N. O sits second to the right of S.
steps: Q at a corner: seat 1. Three persons between M and Q: M at 5 or 6.
T is second to M's right (-2): M 5 gives T 3; M 6 gives T 4.
R = P - 1, and R is not next to Q (1) or M. M 5: R is 7 or 8. M 6: R is 3 or 8, and R 3 puts P on T, so R 8, P 9.
M 5, R 7, P 8: O = S - 2 and U = N - 3 in seats 2, 4, 6, 9: S 4, O 2, N 9, U 6. Every other try in all three branches leaves U or O on a taken seat.
Check: U (6) is third to the right of N (9 - 3 = 6). Fine.
example.answer: Seats 1 to 9 clockwise from the top corner: Q, O, T, S, M, U, R, P, N (corners Q, S, R).

check.q: Nine persons sit round a triangular table facing the centre, corners at seats 1, 4 and 7. A sits at seat 1. B sits fourth to the left of A. Where does B sit?
check.why: Facing the centre, left is +1: 1 + 4 = seat 5, the first side seat after corner 4. "Seat 4" is a step of three, the tempting slip of counting A's own seat.

shortcut.title: Corner to corner is three
text: On the nine-seat table, from a corner a step of 3 lands on the next corner, and a step of 6 on the last one.
So "two persons between X and Y" with X at a corner, or "Y is third to the left of X", puts Y at a corner without drawing.

lessons.title: No one at the corners
lessons.plain: New: the persons sit only along the sides, two or three to a side. Neighbours across a corner are still neighbours, but they are on different sides.
teach: Three of the 28 bank puzzles leave the corners empty of seats: two or three persons on each side.
**How to draw it.** Number the seats clockwise as usual, and draw a short bar between the sides: with two a side, the sides are 1-2, 3-4, 5-6; with three a side, 1-2-3, 4-5-6, 7-8-9.
**What changes.** There is no seat type now, so the parity trick is gone. Instead you get a **side** for each person.
- "X and Y sit on the same side" picks one of the pairs (or triples).
- "X and Y are neighbours but not on the same side" puts them at the two ends of a corner: one at the end of a side, the other at the start of the next.
- "X is second to the left of Y" on a two-a-side table puts X in the same place on the next side.
**Where to start.** All three sides look the same, so seat the most-mentioned person on side 1. Try them at the first seat of the side and at the last seat: two cases.
Bank warning: in the set used for practice, the question "who is related to P" is keyed as "who is to P as L is to O", the reverse of the usual reading. The working shows both.

example.q: Original example, checked by script. Six persons A to F sit round a triangular table, two on each side and no one at a corner, all facing the centre. D sits second to the left of B. A and B sit on the same side. C and D sit on the same side. F sits on the immediate right of A.
steps: Sides are 1-2, 3-4, 5-6. Left is +1.
Try B at the second seat of a side, seat 2: D = 2 + 2 = 4. A shares B's side: A 1. C shares D's side: C 3. F is A's immediate right: 1 - 1 = seat 6. E takes 5.
Try B at the first seat, seat 1: D 3, A 2, C 4, and F = 2 - 1 = seat 1, which is B's. Out.
example.answer: Seats 1 to 6: A, B | C, D | E, F.

lessons.title: One seat is empty
lessons.plain: New: one seat has no one in it. Count it when a clue counts seats or places; skip it when a clue counts persons.
teach: Four of the 28 bank puzzles have one empty seat: five persons on six seats, or eight on nine.
**The one rule.** The empty seat is a seat, not a person.
| The clue says | Count |
| "second to the left", "two places away", "two seats between" | seats, the empty one included |
| "two persons sit between", "how many persons" | persons only, skip the empty seat |
| "immediate neighbour" | the seat next door; if that seat is empty, they are not neighbours |
**The empty seat still faces somewhere.** It faces the way its seat type faces. "Who sits on the immediate right of the vacant seat" uses that seat's right.

**Persons-between clues are loose.** "Three persons sit between E and D" can be true across four seats if one of them is empty. So count the seats on each side and ask where the empty seat can go; a clue like "D does not sit next to the empty seat" then settles it.
A check by script: in Drill 4 of the Quick revision tab, reading "one person between" as "one seat between" gives no arrangement at all; the persons-only reading gives exactly one.

example.q: Bank set (Guidely triangular vacant, set 1, questions 11 to 15). Eight persons M to T sit round a triangular table with nine seats: one at each corner, facing the centre, and two on each side, facing away. One seat is empty. T sits on the immediate right of M, who sits on a side. Q sits second to the right of T. S sits two places away from Q. Two persons sit between S and O, who does not sit next to T. R sits fourth to the right of O. One person sits between R and P. N does not sit at a corner.
steps: Corners 1, 4, 7 face in (left +1); side seats face out (left -1, right +1).
M is on a side and faces out, so T, on M's right, is M + 1. Try M at seat 2: T 3, and Q = 3 + 2 = 5. S is two seats from Q: 7 (3 is T).

Two persons between S (7) and O, O not next to T: O at 1, with 8 and 9 both persons. O faces in, so R = 1 - 4 = seat 6. One person between R and P: P 8 (P 4 would need the empty seat between S and O). N on a side: N 9. The empty seat is 4.
Starting M at seat 3 instead (T then at the corner 4) runs to the end and the last clues leave no seat for P or N. Out.
example.answer: Seats 1 to 9: O, M, T, empty, Q, R, S, P, N. O and S sit at corners facing the centre; the rest face outside.

lessons.title: Other shapes: the same counting
lessons.plain: Insurance: pentagon and hexagon tables. Number the seats round the shape and everything from the triangle carries over; only the size and the meaning of "opposite" change.
teach: Your Guidely bank also has 24 pentagon puzzles and 24 hexagon puzzles. None was seen in the papers either, so this lesson is short. I solved five of them by script; all five had one arrangement and their keys matched, apart from one "related" question keyed the reverse way.
**The same method.** Number the seats clockwise from the top. If there are corners and middles, odd seats are corners and even seats middles, so the parity trick works unchanged.
| Table | Seats | Opposite |
| Pentagon, corners only | 5 | none |
| Pentagon, corners and middles | 10 | 5 seats on: a corner faces a middle |
| Hexagon, corners only | 6 | 3 seats on |
| Hexagon, corners and middles | 12 | 6 seats on: corner faces corner |
On a 12-seat hexagon, "faces" often means opposite. On a 5-seat pentagon there is no opposite, so options built on it are traps.
Second facts (companies, juices, bikes) and empty seats work exactly as in lessons 3 and 6.

example.q: Bank set (Guidely pentagonal two-variable, set 1, questions 11 to 15; one clue is printed inside question 11). Five persons P, Q, R, S, T sit at the five corners of a pentagonal table facing the centre. Their bikes are KTM, Hero, TVS, Bajaj and Royal Enfield. T has Hero and sits second to the right of S. The KTM owner sits next to S. R does not sit next to S. Q does not sit next to R. The Royal Enfield owner sits on the immediate left of the TVS owner. Neither S nor P has TVS.
steps: Seats 1 to 5 clockwise; left +1. T = S - 2: put S at 5, T at 3.
R is not next to S (4 or 1): R 2. Q is not next to R (1 or 3): Q 4. P takes 1.
Royal Enfield = TVS + 1, TVS not S or P, and T has Hero: TVS on R (2) puts Royal Enfield on T. So TVS on Q (4), Royal Enfield on S (5).
KTM is next to S: P (1). R has Bajaj.
example.answer: Seats 1 to 5: P KTM, R Bajaj, T Hero, Q TVS, S Royal Enfield.
